title: No. 3 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence) (Jay)
paragraphs: It is not a new observation that the people of any country—if, like the Americans, they are intelligent and well-informed—rarely adopt and steadily hold an erroneous opinion about their interests for many years. That fact naturally creates great respect for the high regard the American people have so long and uniformly held for the importance of remaining firmly united under one federal government, equipped with sufficient powers for all general and national purposes.
The more carefully I consider and investigate the reasons that seem to have given rise to this opinion, the more convinced I become that they are sound and conclusive.

Among the many concerns to which a wise and free people must direct their attention, providing for their SAFETY seems to be the first. The SAFETY of the people relates to a great variety of circumstances and considerations, and therefore allows great latitude to those who wish to define it precisely and comprehensively.

For the moment, I mean to consider it only as it relates to the preservation of peace and tranquility, both against dangers from FOREIGN ARMS AND INFLUENCE and against dangers of the LIKE KIND arising from domestic causes. Since the former comes first in order, it is fitting to discuss it first. Let us therefore examine whether the people are not right in their opinion that a cordial Union, under an effective national government, gives them the best security that can be devised against HOSTILITIES from abroad.

The number of wars that have happened or will happen in the world will always be in proportion to the number and weight of the causes—whether REAL or PRETENDED—that PROVOKE or INVITE them. If this remark is correct, it becomes useful to ask whether so many JUST causes of war are likely to be given by UNITED AMERICA as by DISUNITED America. For if it turns out that United America will probably give the fewest, then in this respect Union most tends to keep the people at peace with other nations.

JUST causes of war, for the most part, arise either from violations of treaties or from direct violence. America has already formed treaties with no fewer than six foreign nations, and all of them, except Prussia, are maritime powers and therefore able to harass and injure us. She also has extensive commerce with Portugal, Spain, and Britain, and with the latter two we must additionally take into account the fact that they are neighbors.

It is of high importance to the peace of America that she observe the laws of nations toward all these powers, and to me it seems clear this will be more perfectly and punctually done by one national government than it could be either by thirteen separate States or by three or four distinct confederacies.

Because once an effective national government is established, the best men in the country will not only consent to serve, but will generally be appointed to manage it. For although town, county, or other narrow influence may place men in State assemblies, senates, courts, or executive offices, a more general and extensive reputation for talent and other qualifications will be necessary to recommend men to offices under the national government—especially as it will have the widest field for choice and never face that shortage of suitable people which is not uncommon in some of the States. Hence the administration, the political counsels, and the judicial decisions of the national government will be wiser, more systematic, and more judicious than those of individual States, and consequently more satisfactory in dealings with other nations, as well as more SAFE for us.

Because, under the national government, treaties and articles of treaties, as well as the laws of nations, will always be interpreted in one sense and executed in the same way—whereas rulings on the same points and questions, in thirteen States or in three or four confederacies, will not always agree or be consistent. This will follow both from the variety of independent courts and judges appointed by different and independent governments, and from the different local laws and interests that may affect and influence them. The wisdom of the convention, in committing such questions to the jurisdiction and judgment of courts appointed by, and answerable only to, one national government, cannot be too highly praised.

Because the prospect of immediate loss or gain may often tempt the governing party in one or two States to depart from good faith and justice. But those temptations, not reaching the other States and therefore having little or no influence on the national government, will fail, and good faith and justice will be preserved. The case of the treaty of peace with Britain adds great weight to this reasoning.

Because, even if the governing party in a State should be willing to resist such temptations, those temptations may, and commonly do, result from circumstances peculiar to the State and may affect a great number of its inhabitants. The governing party may not always be able, even if willing, to prevent the planned injustice or to punish the offenders. But the national government, not being affected by such local circumstances, will neither be tempted to commit the wrong itself, nor lack the power or willingness to prevent or punish its commission by others.

So far, then, as either deliberate or accidental violations of treaties and the laws of nations provide JUST causes of war, they are less to be feared under one general government than under several smaller ones, and in that respect the former most favors the SAFETY of the people.

As for those just causes of war that arise from direct and unlawful violence, it seems equally clear to me that one good national government provides far more security against dangers of that kind than can come from any other source.

Because such acts of violence are more often caused by the passions and interests of a part than of the whole; of one or two States than of the Union. Not a single Indian war has yet been caused by the aggressions of the present federal government, weak as it is. But there are several instances of Indian hostilities provoked by the improper conduct of individual States, who—either unable or unwilling to restrain or punish offenses—have given occasion for the slaughter of many innocent inhabitants.

The proximity of Spanish and British territories, bordering some States and not others, naturally confines the causes of quarrel more directly to the borderers. The bordering States, if any, will be the ones who, under the impulse of sudden irritation and a quick sense of apparent interest or injury, will be most likely to provoke war with these nations through direct violence. Nothing can so effectively prevent that danger as a national government, whose wisdom and prudence will not be diminished by the passions that drive the parties immediately involved.

But the national government will not only give fewer just causes of war; it will also be better able to settle them amicably. It will be more temperate and cool, and in that respect, as well as in others, will be more capable of acting deliberately than the offending State. The pride of states, like that of men, naturally disposes them to justify all their actions and resists their acknowledging, correcting, or repairing their errors and offenses. The national government, in such cases, will not be affected by this pride, but will proceed with moderation and candor to consider and decide on the means most fitting to extricate them from the difficulties that threaten them.

Besides, it is well known that acknowledgments, explanations, and compensations are often accepted as satisfactory from a strong, united nation, while they would be rejected as unsatisfactory if offered by a State or confederacy of little weight or power.

In 1685, the state of Genoa, having offended Louis XIV, tried to appease him. He demanded that they send their Doge, or chief magistrate, accompanied by four of their senators, to FRANCE to ask his pardon and receive his terms. They were forced to comply for the sake of peace. Would he, on any occasion, either have demanded or have accepted such humiliation from Spain, Britain, or any other POWERFUL nation?
